stories.headline: Garment unrest enters fourth day as 200 more factories close
stories.summary: Garment workers' protests entered a fourth day on 3 November, with at least 200 factories in Savar and Ashulia closed and 264 in Savar-Ashulia plus 150 in Gazipur shut the day before. Police filed cases against more than 2,300 people in Savar and arrested 33 Awami League-affiliated people in Dhaka over alleged sabotage while posing as garment workers. About 50 police personnel were injured in clashes over four days.
stories.why_it_matters: The unrest is now a multi-day crisis hitting the export sector; the arrests and cases show how the state is responding, and the wage demand remains unresolved.
stories.exam_facts: Protests entered fourth day on 3 November; 200 factories closed in Savar-Ashulia on 3 November; 264 shut in Savar-Ashulia and 150 in Gazipur on 2 November; 3 cases filed in Savar against 2,300+ people; 33 AL-affiliated people arrested in Dhaka over alleged sabotage; about 50 police injured in four days; last wage rise from Tk 8,000 to Tk 12,500 took effect 1 December 2023.
stories.exam_relevance: High — RMG, labour unrest, law and order.
stories.key_people: Salahuddin Ahmed, Home Minister; Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, Superintendent, Ashulia Industrial Police-1; Akhter Hossain, Deputy Commissioner (Media), Dhaka Metropolitan Police.
stories.figures: 200 factories closed (3 November); 264 + 150 shut (2 November); 2,300+ accused; 33 arrested; about 50 police injured.

stories.headline: Wage board yet to hold first meeting three days after formation
stories.summary: The six-member garment wage board formed on 1 November has yet to hold its first meeting three days later, even as protests continued in Gazipur, Savar-Ashulia and Mirpur. Chairman Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman said a meeting would be held soon and the process would be completed much faster than the previous board, which took 45 days to meet and six to seven months to finish. Analysis shows inflation has outpaced wage growth since February 2022, so a fair wage would be at least Tk 17,500 just to restore real income.
stories.why_it_matters: The wage board is the institutional answer to the unrest; its delay and the economics of a fair wage are the heart of the story and of labour-policy exams.
stories.exam_facts: Wage board formed 1 November, no first meeting by 3 November; chairman Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman; previous board: first meeting after 45 days, process took six to seven months; inflation 8.34 percent (September 2026) vs wage growth 8.05 percent (August); inflation outpaced wage growth since February 2022; fair wage at least Tk 17,500 to restore real income, Tk 18,000 to keep the shortfall within Tk 3,000.
stories.exam_relevance: High — wage board, inflation, labour economics.
stories.key_people: Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman, Chairman of the wage board; Mosleh Uddin Ahmed, independent member.
stories.figures: No meeting in 3 days; fair wage at least Tk 17,500; inflation 8.34 percent; wage growth 8.05 percent.

stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections
stories.summary: The United States attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on 2 November, the Wall Street Journal reported, even as President Donald Trump signalled progress in negotiations with Tehran to end the eight-month-old conflict. Iranian state media reported five explosions in rapid succession on the island, the largest in the Strait of Hormuz. The strike was the latest in a series of limited US strikes carried out secretly in recent weeks, and oil prices plunged more than 7 percent on optimism over a possible deal.
stories.why_it_matters: A US strike on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz — the world's key oil corridor — affects energy prices, trade and Bangladesh's import bill, and is a major international-affairs story.
stories.exam_facts: Strike on Qeshm Island, 2 November (reported by the Wall Street Journal, citing US officials); five explosions reported by Iranian agency IRNA; latest of secret limited US strikes over recent weeks; Strait of Hormuz largely blocked since the war began in late February; oil prices fell more than 7 percent on 2 November; Trump said a deal with Tehran 'could happen'.
stories.exam_relevance: High — US-Iran conflict, Strait of Hormuz, oil prices.
stories.figures: Five explosions reported; oil prices down more than 7 percent; war eight months old.

stories.headline: Americans vote in midterm elections that could upend Trump's presidency
stories.summary: Americans voted on 3 November in midterm elections that threaten to break Donald Trump's grip on Washington, with Democrats poised to seize the House and challenge for the Senate. All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four Senate seats to take both chambers, with Trump's approval rating near the low 30s amid anger over living costs and the war against Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: Midterm results decide who controls the US Congress and therefore trade, aid and foreign policy that affect Bangladesh; the numbers are standard international-affairs material.
stories.exam_facts: Midterms on 3 November 2026; all 435 House seats, 35 of 100 Senate seats, governors in 36 states; Democrats need +3 House seats and net +4 Senate seats; Trump's approval near the low 30s; midterms are held at the halfway point between presidential elections and are often a referendum on the president.
stories.key_people: Donald Trump, US President; Jon Ossoff, Democratic Senator (Georgia).
stories.figures: 435 House seats; 35 Senate seats; 36 governorships; Democrats need +3 House and +4 Senate.

stories.headline: Amit Shah claims three crore 'Bangladeshi infiltrators' in India's voter rolls
stories.summary: India's Home Minister Amit Shah claimed that around three crore people flagged during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls were Bangladeshi infiltrators with no legitimate place on the rolls. The Commission's draft data classified about 3.01 crore entries as voters who were absent or untraceable, but it has not identified all of them as Bangladeshi nationals, and the figures remain subject to claims and objections. Shah challenged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi to a parliamentary debate on the revision.
stories.why_it_matters: Claims about Bangladeshi migrants in India are a sensitive bilateral issue; the distinction between the minister's claim and the Commission's data is exactly what exam questions test.
stories.exam_facts: Claim: about three crore flagged people are Bangladeshi infiltrators (Amit Shah, at a BJP rally in Hyderabad); Election Commission draft data: about 3.01 crore entries absent or untraceable, not identified as Bangladeshi; Shah said 6.25 crore had shifted residences, three crore were deceased, one crore had duplicate entries; exercise: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
stories.key_people: Amit Shah, India's Union Home Minister; Rahul Gandhi, Congress leader.
stories.figures: Three crore claimed as infiltrators; 3.01 crore entries absent or untraceable (EC draft data).

stories.headline: Private sector credit growth falls to lowest on record
stories.summary: Private sector credit growth fell to a historic low of 4.17 percent in September, down from 4.75 percent in August, according to provisional Bangladesh Bank data — the weakest since at least 1993 — and below the central bank's projection of 6.8 percent through December. Bankers blamed weak business confidence, shelved investment plans and cautious lending. Inflation eased slightly to 8.34 percent in September, though the IMF projected average inflation to rise to 10.9 percent this fiscal year.
stories.why_it_matters: Credit growth is the key gauge of investment and business confidence; a record low signals a weak economy and is a core banking-exam indicator.
stories.exam_facts: Private sector credit growth: 4.17 percent in September (from 4.75 percent in August); lowest since at least 1993; Bangladesh Bank projection: 6.8 percent through December; inflation 8.34 percent in September (from 8.26 percent in August); IMF projected average inflation of 10.9 percent in the current fiscal year.
stories.key_people: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Managing Director and CEO, Mutual Trust Bank.
stories.figures: 4.17 percent credit growth (September); lowest since at least 1993; inflation 8.34 percent; IMF projection 10.9 percent.

stories.headline: Bangladesh Bank appoints independent directors to two troubled banks
stories.summary: Bangladesh Bank appointed five independent directors to the boards of two troubled lenders, Bangladesh Commerce Bank and The Premier Bank, using its powers under the Bank Companies Act, 1991. Md Rafiqul Islam and SM Abdul Hamid will join Commerce Bank, while Brigadier General (retired) Md Jahedur Rahman, Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain and Md Masudur Rahman Shah will join Premier Bank. Commerce Bank had about 65 percent non-performing loans at the end of 2025, and Premier Bank 31 percent.
stories.why_it_matters: Central-bank intervention in weak banks is a core banking-reform topic; the NPL ratios show the scale of the problem.
stories.exam_facts: Five independent directors appointed under the Bank Companies Act, 1991; Commerce Bank: Md Rafiqul Islam and SM Abdul Hamid; Premier Bank: Brig Gen (retd) Md Jahedur Rahman, Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain, Md Masudur Rahman Shah; Commerce Bank NPL about 65 percent (end-2025), losses Tk 450 crore; Premier Bank NPL 31 percent, losses nearly Tk 1,000 crore in 2025.
stories.exam_relevance: High — banking regulation, NPL, Bangladesh Bank.
stories.figures: Five directors; Commerce Bank NPL about 65 percent; Premier Bank NPL 31 percent; losses Tk 450 crore and about Tk 1,000 crore.

stories.headline: BNP factional clashes killed 9 and injured 185 in October, report says
stories.summary: Internal feuds within the BNP accounted for half of all political violence in October, leaving nine people dead and at least 185 injured in 35 clashes, according to the Human Rights Support Society. Overall, at least 12 people — 10 from the BNP and two from the Awami League — were killed and 334 injured in 70 incidents of political violence. The report also recorded 33 mob beatings that killed 22 people, attacks on 46 journalists, and violence against 261 women and girls, including 82 rapes.
stories.why_it_matters: Monthly political-violence data is a governance exam staple, and the figures show the scale of intra-party violence and attacks on journalists and women.
stories.exam_facts: October political violence: 70 incidents, 12 killed (10 BNP, 2 AL), 334 injured; BNP factional clashes: 35 incidents, 9 dead, 185 injured; 33 mob beatings killed 22; 46 journalists attacked or harassed in 28 incidents (1 killed, 31 injured); 261 women and girls subjected to violence, including 82 rapes (42 children) and 20 gang rapes; source: Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), compiled from 16 media outlets.
stories.exam_relevance: High — political violence, human rights, governance.
stories.key_people: Ijajul Islam, Executive Director, Human Rights Support Society.
stories.figures: 9 dead, 185 injured in BNP factional clashes; 12 killed, 334 injured overall; 22 killed in mob beatings; 82 rapes.

stories.headline: Bangladesh and South Korea plan joint investment task force
stories.summary: Bangladesh and South Korea agreed to set up a joint government-private sector working group to identify investment opportunities and expand trade, following the conclusion of negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury told his South Korean counterpart in Seoul that cooperation should move beyond textiles into electronics and semiconductors, shipbuilding, renewable energy, artificial intelligence and digital industries.
stories.why_it_matters: A new economic partnership with South Korea and the move beyond garments into technology are trade and foreign-policy exam topics.
stories.exam_facts: Joint working group agreed after conclusion of CEPA (Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement) negotiations; meeting in Seoul between Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury and South Korean Trade Minister Jung-sung Park; priority areas: electronics and semiconductors, shipbuilding, renewable energy, AI, digital industries; customs duties on electronics raw materials cut from 26 percent to zero.
stories.key_people: Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Finance and Planning Minister; Jung-sung Park, South Korean Trade Minister.
stories.figures: Customs duties on electronics raw materials cut from 26 percent to zero.

stories.headline: Prosecutors move to seize Hasina and Asaduzzaman's properties
stories.summary: The Chief Prosecutor's Office wrote to the Home Ministry to take control of all movable and immovable properties of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina and former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan, who were sentenced to death by the International Crimes Tribunal on 17 November 2025 for crimes against humanity. The tribunal ordered the seizure of their assets, with half to be identified and seized first and the proceeds distributed to the families of those killed in the July uprising, through the July Foundation or another statutory body.
stories.why_it_matters: The confiscation of a convicted former prime minister's assets is a landmark legal and governance story; the dates, the tribunal and the compensation plan are directly askable.
stories.exam_facts: Sentenced to death on 17 November 2025 by International Crimes Tribunal-1 for crimes against humanity; tribunal ordered seizure of all properties; Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam wrote to the Home Ministry on 3 November; half of the assets to be identified and seized first, sold by auction or other legal means; proceeds to families of July uprising martyrs and victims.
stories.key_people: Md Aminul Islam, Chief Prosecutor; Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan (convicted fugitives).
stories.figures: Death sentences on 17 November 2025; half of assets to be seized first.

stories.headline: Government eyes 3,000-4,000MW solar addition before next summer
stories.summary: The government expects to add 3,000 to 4,000 megawatts of solar power to the national grid before next summer, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said while opening the first-ever Solar Expo-2026 in Dhaka. The government targets 20 percent of electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and 30 percent by 2040, has allocated Tk 1,500 crore for solar financing, and will buy surplus rooftop power at Tk 10.50 per unit by February 2027 under a special net-metering arrangement.
stories.why_it_matters: Renewable energy targets and financing are energy-policy exam topics, and the solar push links climate goals with reducing dependence on imported fuel.
stories.exam_facts: Solar addition target: 3,000-4,000MW before next summer; renewable targets: 20 percent by 2030, 30 percent by 2040; Tk 1,500 crore allocated for solar financing; net-metering buyback Tk 10.50 per unit by February 2027; Solar Expo-2026 theme: 'Utilise Every Inch of Rooftop, Increase Income through Solar Power'; Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance 2026.
stories.key_people: Tarique Rahman, Prime Minister; Iqbal Hassan Mahmood Tuku, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister.
stories.figures: 3,000-4,000MW before next summer; 20 percent by 2030; 30 percent by 2040; Tk 1,500 crore; Tk 10.50 per unit.

stories.headline: Bangladesh's demographic window is narrowing, World Bank warns
stories.summary: Bangladesh risks missing the economic benefits of its large working-age population as slow job creation, low female labour force participation and skills shortages hold back productivity, a World Bank report says. The working-age population share is projected to peak in 2045, and Bangladesh is projected to become an aged society by 2051. About 84 percent of the workforce — roughly 58 million people — are employed in the informal sector.
stories.why_it_matters: The demographic dividend is a core development-economics topic; the peak year, the informal-sector share and the ageing date are directly askable.
stories.exam_facts: Report: 'Demographic Change in South Asia: From Tailwinds to Headwinds for Development' (World Bank); working-age population share to peak in 2045; aged society by 2051 (people 65+ a larger share); about 84 percent of the workforce in the informal sector (about 58 million people); reforms needed in jobs, skills, healthcare and social protection.
stories.key_people: Franziska Ohnsorge, Chief Economist for Asia, World Bank.
stories.figures: Working-age share peaks 2045; aged society by 2051; 84 percent informal (about 58 million people).

stories.headline: Plan to split the National Board of Revenue back on the table
stories.summary: The government may split the National Board of Revenue into two separate divisions — a Revenue Implementation Division and a Revenue Policy Division — under a bill likely to be placed before the upcoming session of parliament, based on a high-level committee's recommendations. The move follows the failure of parliament to ratify the interim government's revenue reform ordinances within the constitutionally mandated 30 days of its first sitting on 12 March, which left them invalid.
stories.why_it_matters: NBR reform is the centrepiece of Bangladesh's revenue and governance reform; the two-division structure and the ordinance history are directly askable.
stories.exam_facts: Proposed split: Revenue Implementation Division (headed by a chairman with secretary rank) and Revenue Policy Division (secretary from general cadre officers, with economists, chartered accountants and legal professionals); bill likely before the upcoming parliament session; committee headed by Ismail Zabiullah, the prime minister's adviser on public administration; 13 ordinances lost validity after parliament failed to ratify them within 30 days of its first sitting on 12 March.
stories.key_people: Ismail Zabiullah, Prime Minister's Adviser on Public Administration (committee head).
stories.figures: Two divisions proposed; 13 ordinances lapsed; 30-day ratification window.

stories.headline: Four global firms vie for Dhaka airport third terminal contract
stories.summary: Four international aviation companies — Menzies Aviation of the UK, Swissport of Switzerland, Çelebi of Türkiye and dnata of the UAE — have been shortlisted to provide ground handling at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport's third terminal. Menzies proposed investing more than $12 million and creating over 1,000 direct jobs. A draft deal would bar other civilian airports within 100km from starting commercial operations for 15 years, even as passenger traffic is projected to reach 33 million by 2045.
stories.why_it_matters: Airport privatisation, foreign investment and the controversial 15-year restriction are infrastructure and competition-policy exam topics.
stories.exam_facts: Shortlisted: Menzies Aviation (UK), Swissport (Switzerland), Çelebi Aviation Holding (Türkiye), dnata (UAE); Menzies proposed over $12 million investment, 1,000+ direct jobs (99 percent local) and about 4,500 indirect jobs; draft deal: 15-year bar on rival civilian airports within 100km; HSIA traffic projected 33 million by 2045 vs capacity 24 million; partial opening of the third terminal targeted for 16 December.
stories.key_people: Air Commodore Abu Sayeed Mehboob Khan, Member (Operations and Planning), Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh.
stories.figures: Four firms shortlisted; over $12 million proposed; 1,000+ direct jobs; 15-year restriction within 100km; 33 million passengers by 2045.
